claims.text: Overall high-temperature wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings is governed by in-situ tribo-oxidation that forms a stable protective oxide layer.
The protective oxide layer reduces direct metal-to-metal contact.
Formation of the oxide layer changes the dominant wear mode to oxidative abrasion or controlled oxide removal.
The relevant structural mediator is a continuous protective oxide film, potentially containing spinel-like phases.
Rapid tribo-oxidation of FeNiCrCoCu at high temperature in an oxidizing environment produces a stable oxide layer.
The stable oxide layer reduces the overall wear rate.
A reciprocating wear regime near 26 N, 40 Hz, 0.5 mm amplitude, and 900 s is suitable for testing elevated-temperature wear behavior.
Wear resistance can increase markedly at 800–900 °C, with particularly high resistance at 900 °C.
The cited elevated-temperature wear trend is applicable to FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings despite being observed in bulk SPS AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5.
At high temperature, FeNiCrCoCu tested in air will have lower wear depth than FeNiCrCoCu tested under inert conditions.
At high temperature, FeNiCrCoCu tested in air will have a lower coefficient of friction than FeNiCrCoCu tested under inert conditions.
XRD and microscopy will reveal a continuous protective oxide layer after wear testing in air.
The protective oxide layer will be absent or incomplete after otherwise equivalent inert-atmosphere testing.
No protective oxide layer develops under room-temperature or inert baseline conditions.
The predicted protective behavior is restricted to approximately 800–900 °C, high load, and an oxidizing environment.
At lower temperatures or under non-oxidizing conditions, the protective oxide may not form.
The oxide's precise composition, structure, and contribution to friction reduction may vary with processing parameters.
Failure to detect a continuous or stable oxide film in air at 900 °C would falsify the proposed mechanism.
Failure of the oxidizing atmosphere to significantly reduce wear depth and coefficient of friction relative to argon would falsify the hypothesis.
